newsitem.title: GERMANY: Italy's Prodi to Bonn amid tough German EMU talk.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Prodi to Bonn amid tough German EMU talk.

text.p: Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi was due to discuss Europe's single currency with Chancellor Helmut Kohl in Bonn on Thursday evening amid continued German pressure for a rock-solid economic and monetary union (EMU).

Prodi's visit follows similar talks between Kohl and Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar near Heidelberg on Tuesday which also focused on efforts by the two Mediterranean states to qualify for EMU at its planned start in 1999.
A Bonn government spokesman said the two men would dine at Kohl's bungalow on the chancellery grounds and no statement was expected afterwards. Prodi was due to return directly to Rome.
The Prodi and Aznar visits came amid continued warnings from Germany's central bank, the Bundesbank, against any budget "window-dressing" to juggle budgets so they meet the stiff criteria for EMU.
EU officials say Italy and Spain have slim chances of meeting all the Maastricht Treaty requirements for EMU despite their recent efforts to tighten fiscal controls to qualify.
The two meetings have fuelled speculation about a possible deal to have Spain and Italy join the commmon European currency soon after 1999, an idea some EU officials favour.
Diplomats said Prodi should expect the same as Aznar got -- encouragement to keep trimming budgets to meet the Maastricht convergence criteria but no further public commitment.
"It is far too early for Kohl to say anything more," said one envoy following the build-up to the new currency bloc.
Otmar Issing, the Bundesbank's chief economist, kept up the central bank's campaign for a rock-solid EMU on Thursday.
"We view with some concern attempts to alter budgetary positions (ahead of EMU)," he told a conference in Luxembourg. "That must not happen."

Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer told the French daily Le Monde on Wednesday that the European Union would have to look at the candidates' long-term economic prospects before accepting them as EMU members.
"All the figures, for example the budget figures, must be fulfilled not on the basis of a massaging of the balance sheet, but in the direction of long-term stability," he said.
Tietmeyer said Italy would be welcome to join the single currency if it fulfils the criteria in a long-term way.

He declined to name any "window-dressers" but economists say France's decision to bolster its new budget with a one-off transfer of funds from state-owned France Telecom set the tone for other countries to try to massage their figures.
Tietmeyer stressed that the lack of a real political union in Europe meant the EMU must have a "culture of stability" to ensure that all members followed the same policies.

Kohl failed to have the 1991 Maastricht treaty include a political union to harmonise national policies once EMU member states could no longer use exchange rates or more deficit spending to help adjust for economic problems.

To correct this, Bonn's Finance Minister Theo Waigel has campaigned hard within the European Union for a "stability pact" with stiff automatic fines for any EMU member that overruns its budget targets.
The European Commission accepted this principle in EMU proposals unveiled on Wednesday but took some of the sting out of them by leaving loopholes to avoid automatic penalities.
German commentators frowned on the compromise, which officials said came about after stiff resistance to automatic fines from several southern European states.
"The stability pact's sanctions mechanism is unconvincing if it is not automatic and the final decision is left up to the finance ministers," the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung wrote.
"This means sinners will judge sinners. One can easily see that absolution without penance will be the usual result."

The business daily Handelsblatt said in its editorial: "The stability pact that was supposed to bind the politicians' hands thus ends up subject to political influence. That's like putting the fox in charge of the henhouse."
